methodological_rigor.justification: This retrospective single-center series of 50 patients with H&N radiation-induced malignancies applies appropriate Kaplan-Meier survival analysis with log-rank testing. The Cahan/Arlen/Murray diagnostic criteria are rigorously applied to define the cohort. Key limitations include incomplete radiotherapy dose and fractionation data for many patients, heterogeneous histologies and treatment modalities, and no multivariate analysis; the small sample size precludes meaningful subgroup analyses. Margin status survival comparison is appropriately caveated given the very small R2 subgroup (n=1).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a retrospective single-institution case series (LoE 4) addressing a rare but clinically important complication of head and neck radiotherapy. The findings—that surgery confers markedly better survival (5-year OS 57.5% vs 0%) and that long-term surveillance is essential—have direct clinical implications for management of this increasing patient population. The rarity of RIMs limits study size, but the 20+ year experience from a major cancer center provides meaningful real-world outcome data.

reporting_quality.justification: The manuscript follows observational reporting conventions reasonably well: study design, setting, inclusion criteria, and statistical methods are clearly described. Survival data are reported with confidence intervals. However, detailed radiotherapy dose/technique data are explicitly acknowledged as unavailable for many patients, and no supplementary data or dataset is deposited publicly. The two illustrative clinical cases are informative. Some heterogeneity in treatment modalities limits comparability across subgroups.

novelty_literature.justification: This study adds to the limited single-institution literature on H&N RIMs with one of the more comprehensive Italian series, spanning 21 years. The finding that smoking alters histologic distribution in RIMs (equal SCC/sarcoma in smokers vs SCC predominance in non-smokers) is a novel observation. However, the primary conclusions—surgery improves survival, young age at RT predicts longer latency—confirm established knowledge from prior smaller series and Asian literature predominantly featuring NPC patients.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is clearly structured and written in fluent English. The two clinical cases effectively illustrate the diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. The discussion is thorough, contextualizing findings against the relevant international literature, and limitations are transparently acknowledged including the inability to perform multivariate analysis and incomplete dosimetric data. Minor issues include some repetition between results and discussion sections.

key_strengths: One of the largest single-institution European series on H&N radiation-induced malignancies with a 21-year follow-up period
Rigorous application of Cahan/Arlen/Murray diagnostic criteria with transparent exclusion rationale
Novel observation on smoking modifying histologic distribution in RIMs, suggesting radiation-driven carcinogenesis overrides tobacco-associated SCC patterns
Clear surgical survival benefit demonstrated (5-year OS 57.5% vs 0%), consistent with prior series, with confidence intervals reported
key_concerns: Small cohort (n=50) with incomplete radiotherapy dosimetry data severely limits subgroup analyses and any conclusions regarding dose-response relationships
Retrospective single-center design with heterogeneous primary tumor sites, histologies, and treatment modalities limits generalizability
No multivariate analysis performed; observed associations (e.g., age at RT and latency) cannot be adjusted for confounders
No data or code deposited in a public repository; raw data not available for independent replication
chief_reviewer.rationale: This well-written retrospective series from a major Italian cancer center provides competent characterization of a rare and clinically important entity, with appropriate limitations disclosure. Tier 3 reflects the incremental but meaningful contribution to the sparse RIM literature; minor revisions should address more systematic reporting of available dosimetric data and clarity on statistical approach.
